about: Windward Maroon town in Portland Parish, founded as New Nanny Town under the 1740 peace treaty and later renamed Moore Town. It is the living successor of Nanny Town, and UNESCO lists its Maroon heritage as world heritage.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage element, the Maroon Heritage of Moore Town (proclaimed 2008), for history and status; GeoNames and Wikipedia for the town location in Portland Parish.

about: Leeward Maroon town in the Cockpit Country of St. Elizabeth Parish, named for the Maroon leader Accompong. Its people won autonomy by treaty with the British in 1739 and still govern their own affairs on their own lands today.
source: Wikipedia and Jamaican Maroon histories for the 1739 treaty town and its continuing Maroon council; OpenStreetMap and Mapcarta place node for the Accompong location.

about: Windward Maroon town on the Buff Bay River in Portland Parish, settled after the peace treaties of 1739 and 1740. Its Asafu Yard and Maroon museum keep Kromanti language, drumming, and treaty history alive in daily life.
source: Jamaican Maroon sources and the Charles Town Maroon community and museum for history; OpenStreetMap place, Charles Town (Maroons), Portland Parish, for location.

about: Maroon town in the hills of St. Mary Parish, one of the four treaty towns that survive in Jamaica. Granted its lands after the Maroon treaties, it has kept its own council and Maroon identity for more than 280 years now.
source: Jamaican Maroon sources for treaty town status and the surviving Maroon council; GeoNames populated place in St. Mary Parish for location.

about: Capital settlement of the Quilombo dos Palmares on the Serra da Barriga in Alagoas, a federation of escaped Africans founded around 1602. Ruled last by Zumbi, it resisted Portuguese attacks for decades before it fell in 1694.
source: Wikipedia article on Cerca do Macaco and material on the Parque Memorial Quilombo dos Palmares for the capital settlement, Zumbi, and the 1694 destruction; Wikipedia coordinates for the Serra da Barriga site.

about: The largest quilombo territory in Brazil, about 253,000 hectares in Goias held by descendants of Africans who lived beyond colonial reach for some 200 years. This pin marks Engenho II, one of its main communities today.
source: Peer-reviewed study of the Kalunga territory (PMC) for the territory size, the three Goias municipalities, and some 200 years of isolation; the Engenho II community coordinates given in the academic literature for the pin.

about: The first free African town in the Americas, founded in the early 1600s by Benkos Bioho, who led escapes from Cartagena. Spain recognized its freedom by royal decree, and its people still speak the Palenquero language.
source: UNESCO recognition (Masterpiece proclamation 2005, Intangible Cultural Heritage list 2008) for the first free African town in the Americas and the Palenquero language; Wikipedia coordinates for the town in Mahates, Bolivar.

about: Free Black town in Veracruz founded by Gaspar Yanga and the maroons who followed him out of slavery. First called San Lorenzo de los Negros, it won legal recognition in the early 1600s and took the name Yanga in 1932.
source: Wikipedia and Veracruz histories for Gaspar Yanga, San Lorenzo de los Negros, early legal recognition, and the 1932 renaming; GeoNames for location.

about: Saamaka Maroon village on the Pikin Rio at the head of the Upper Suriname River in the forest interior, and seat of the gaanman, the Saramaka paramount chief. Its people descend from Africans who won freedom by treaty in the 1760s.
source: Wikipedia entry for Asidonhopo (also spelled Asindoopo) for the Saramaka gaanman residence on the Pikin Rio in Sipaliwini District; coordinates from the same gazetteer entry.

about: Aluku (Boni) Maroon commune on the Lawa River in western French Guiana, across from Suriname, and seat of the Aluku granman. The Aluku descend from maroons led by Boni who crossed from Suriname; they became French citizens in 1891.
source: Wikipedia entry for the Papaichton commune for the Aluku (Boni) capital, the granman seat, and the Lawa River location; commune coordinates from the same entry.

about: Garifuna town on the Stann Creek coast of Belize, settled by Garifuna families in the early 1800s and now the district capital. Called the culture capital of Belize, it anchors Garifuna Settlement Day each November 19.
source: Belize and Garifuna sources for the Garifuna settlement, culture capital status, and Settlement Day; OpenStreetMap and GeoNames for the town location at the mouth of Stann Creek.

about: Garifuna village on the Stann Creek coast of Belize, often called the cultural center of the Garifuna people in the country. Drumming, the Garifuna language, and Yurumein traditions remain strong in daily life here.
source: Wikipedia and Belize sources for the Garifuna village and cultural center claim; GeoNames populated place point for location, consistent with a Belize Tourism Board survey point for the village.

about: Traditional Garifuna village on the Caribbean coast of Honduras, about 15 kilometers east of La Ceiba in Atlantida. One of the largest Garifuna communities in Honduras, it is known for drumming and its June fair each year.
source: Garifuna and Honduras sources for the traditional village east of La Ceiba; GeoNames for location. Note: the Wikipedia infobox point sits about 5 km east of the GeoNames point; GeoNames is used here.

about: Garifuna town at the mouth of the Rio Dulce on Guatemala's Caribbean coast, the heart of Garifuna culture in the country. Tradition credits its founding to Marcos Sanchez Diaz, a Black officer from Haiti, in the early 1800s.
source: Garifuna scholarship (Gonzalez; Castillo Valenzuela) for the founding tradition of Marcos Sanchez Diaz and the Garifuna settlement; Wikipedia for the town coordinates at the mouth of the Rio Dulce. Founding year is given as 1802, 1806, or 1831 across sources.

about: Caribbean port in Panama founded by Spain in 1597, built and worked by enslaved Africans and later home to free Cimarron communities. Its Afro-Panamanian Congo culture, festivals, and churches keep that history alive.
source: UNESCO state of conservation reporting for the town coordinates (N9 33 14, W79 39 21); Bowie State University Journal of International Studies and Panama sources for the Cimarron and Congo culture history.

about: Village in southwest New Providence founded in 1831 for Africans freed from slave ships, beginning with 157 people taken from the Portuguese ship Rosa. Its people built St. James Anglican Church with their own hands.
source: Wikipedia entry for Adelaide Village, Bahamas, for the 1831 founding under Governor Sir James Carmichael-Smyth, the 157 Africans freed from the Rosa, and the community-built church; coordinates from the same entry.

about: The first village in Guyana bought by freed Africans, on the East Coast Demerara: in November 1839, eighty-three former slaves from five estates pooled their savings to buy Plantation Northbrook, and renamed it Victoria for the queen.
source: Wikipedia entry for Victoria, Guyana, for the November 1839 purchase of Plantation Northbrook by 83 ex-slaves and the renaming; coordinates from the same entry, East Coast Demerara.

about: Port town on the Samana Peninsula settled from 1824 by free African American families who emigrated under Haiti's open-door policy. Their descendants, the Samana Americans, still speak Samana English and worship in AME churches.
source: Scholarship on the Samana Americans for the 1824 emigration under President Boyer, Samana English, and the AME and Wesleyan churches; Mapcarta and OpenStreetMap with harbor tide station data for the town location.

about: Anchor pin for the Afro-Ecuadorian maroon territory of Esmeraldas, where Alonso de Illescas, a survivor of a 1553 slave ship wreck, governed a free Black territory that stayed beyond Spanish rule for about sixty years.
source: Encyclopedia.com and Afro-Ecuadorian histories for Alonso de Illescas and the free Black territory that stayed outside Spanish domination; Wikipedia for the modern city at the mouth of the Esmeraldas River, used as the anchor pin for the territory.

about: Historic free Black quarter of Frederiksted, St. Croix, established in 1750 as one of the first neighborhoods where free people of African descent could own land and houses, run businesses, and build independent lives.
source: CHANT (Cruzan Heritage and Nature Tourism) Free Gut Frederiksted project, with the National Park Service and the Virgin Islands SHPO as partners, for the 1750 free Black quarter; Wikipedia and GeoNames for the Frederiksted town coordinates. District, not a town.

about: Founded in 1783 beside Shelburne, Nova Scotia, by Black Loyalists evacuated after the American Revolution. For a time it was the largest free settlement of Africans in North America; a heritage centre marks the site.
source: Wikipedia and the Black Loyalist Heritage Society for the 1783 Black Loyalist settlement and its scale; coordinates from the same sources; the site is a National Historic Site.

about: Black community on the shore of Bedford Basin in Halifax, settled by Black families from the 1830s onward. The city demolished it and moved its people in the 1960s; the site is now a National Historic Site and museum.
source: Wikipedia and Africville Museum sources for the community history, the 1960s demolition and relocation, and the 2010 city apology; coordinates for the Africville site on Bedford Basin.

about: Prairie settlement in northern Alberta founded in 1910 and 1911 by Black homesteaders from Oklahoma led by Parson H. Sneed, fleeing Jim Crow. First called Pine Creek, it was Alberta's largest Black community of its era.
source: Alberta heritage sources and GeoNames and OpenStreetMap for the 1910 to 1911 Black homesteader settlement led by Parson H. Sneed; the Obadiah Place heritage site anchors the location.

about: Historic dockland district of Cardiff, Wales, where Black sailors from Africa and the Caribbean settled from the early 1800s and built one of Britain's oldest Black communities around the port. A district, not a town.
source: Wikipedia entry for Tiger Bay for the dockland district and its Black community history; district coordinates from the same entry. District, not a town.

about: District of Liverpool, England, home to Britain's oldest Black community, rooted in the 1730s and grown by Black Loyalists, sailors, and soldiers over ten generations. The Granby streets are its heart. A district, not a town.
source: Wikipedia article, Black people in Liverpool, and the National Lottery Heritage Fund L8 project for Britain's oldest Black community in Toxteth; WeRelate, using the Getty Thesaurus of Geographic Names, for the Toxteth coordinates. District, not a town.

about: Maroon territory in the Bahoruco Mountains along the Haiti and Dominican border. The Maniel maroons were the only maroon community officially recognized in Saint-Domingue, winning terms in 1785. A territory, not a town.
source: Cambridge University Press, Rituals, Runaways, and the Haitian Revolution, for the Maniel as the only officially recognized maroon community of Saint-Domingue and the 1785 terms; Wikipedia coordinates for the Sierra de Bahoruco, used as the territory anchor. Territory, not a town.

about: Freetown, Sierra Leone: built in 1792 by Black settlers, many formerly enslaved, who elected tithingmen and hundreders as their local representatives.
source: University of New Brunswick Loyalist Collection sessional papers for the 1792 founding and settler elections; Geodatos for coordinates.

about: Monrovia, Liberia: founded in 1822 by freed people from the United States. It became the capital of the independent Liberian republic in 1847.
source: Wikipedia and Wikidata for the 1822 founding by emancipated slaves and free Black settlers and the 1847 independence; coordinates from the same reference.

about: Harper, Liberia: settled from 1834 by freed African Americans. As capital of the Republic of Maryland, it was an independent Black-governed state from 1854 to 1857.
source: Wikipedia and Wikidata for Harper and the Republic of Maryland (independent 1854 to 1857); coordinates from the same reference.

about: Sao Joao dos Angolares, Sao Tome and Principe: an Angolar maroon-descendant town whose people elected their own king and ran their communal affairs.
source: Peer-reviewed research (Lorenzino, Portuguese Studies Review, 2007) for the Angolares as an independent community electing their own king; Geodatos for coordinates.

about: Tabon community, Accra, Ghana: Afro-Brazilian former slaves settled here from 1836, received land, and kept their own chiefs and stool. Pin: Brazil House.
source: Scholarship on the Tabon returnee community (von Hesse and Yarak; Schaumloeffel) for the 1836 settlement, land grant, and Tabon chiefs; Vymaps and Google Maps for the Brazil House, Jamestown anchor.

about: Le Morne, Mauritius: escaped slaves formed free communities in this mountain fortress. UNESCO lists it as a symbol of maroon resistance to slavery.
source: UNESCO inscription of the Le Morne Cultural Landscape (2008) for the maroon refuge history; UNESCO site coordinates via Wikipedia.

about: Cirque de Mafate, Reunion: a remote cirque settled by escaped slaves in the 1800s and named for a maroon leader. Its camps were led by their own chiefs.
source: Mafate reference material for the maroon settlement and naming; Mapcarta (OpenStreetMap, GeoNames, Wikidata) for the cirque coordinates. A landscape site, not a town.

about: Madina do Boe, Guinea-Bissau: PAIGC fighters expelled the Portuguese garrison in 1969. In 1973 the elected People's National Assembly declared independence here.
source: Wikipedia entries for Boe and the Guinea-Bissau War of Independence for the 1969 expulsion and the September 1973 assembly and declaration; coordinates from the same reference.
